items.content: The train lurches forward with a groan, pressing bodies together like pages in a waterlogged book. She grips the overhead bar and watches a man's newspaper flutter against her wrist, his headlines bleeding into her morning. Someone smells of coffee, someone else of last night's regret. The tunnel swallows them whole, and for a moment they are all the same — suspended, anonymous, hurtling through the dark toward lives that don't yet know they're coming.

items.content: The last day always arrived with a particular heaviness, the way late afternoon light thickens and turns gold before surrendering to dark. You rode your bicycle slower than usual, memorizing the familiar cracks in the sidewalk, the neighbor's sprinkler catching the sun in brief, brilliant arcs. Supper tasted different that evening — ordinary food made strange by the knowledge that tomorrow would divide your life once more into the measured, clockwork hours of school. You lay in bed listening to summer's last sounds, the cicadas and distant laughter, already becoming memory before the night was even finished.

items.content: The world below arranges itself into something almost painfully orderly from this height — the boats reduced to white punctuation marks on a blue page, the coastline curling away in both directions like a sentence with no end. The wind up here has its own vocabulary, speaking in low, persistent tones against the glass. Far out, where the sea loses its color and borrows the sky's, the horizon holds itself perfectly still, indifferent and absolute, the way only forever can.
